text: Remember the trading company from the start? Here it is.
On the last day of 1600, Queen Elizabeth I gave a charter to a group of London merchants, the East India Company.
At first, they just wanted to trade, and what they wanted most was that Indian cloth, painted printed cotton,
so popular in England that its names entered the English language, calico from Calicut, and chintz from the Hindi, Chint.
It sold so well that English weavers rioted and Parliament passed laws to ban Indian printed
cloth.
The company set up trading posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta.
Bombay, by the way, came to England as part of a royal wedding dowry when a Portuguese
princess married King Charles II.
Imagine getting Mumbai as a wedding gift.
To protect its trade, the company hired soldiers.
soldiers, then more soldiers, then a lot more. Profits look good this year. Excellent, sir.
And this line here, cannons, elephants, regiments. Oh, that's the army. We're a trading company.
Why do we have an army? Why don't the others? By the early 1800s, the company's private
army in India was about 200,000 strong, bigger than the British army itself.
Its rise began with a bored young clerk in Madras who found out he was much better at
war than at paperwork, Robert Clive.
In 1757, at Place in Bengal, Clive's small army faced the Nawab of Bengal.
But Clive had already made a secret deal with the Nawab's own commander.
When the battle began, much of the Nawab's army simply stood still.
One of the most important battles in Indian history was won by a deal.
Within a few years, the company won the right to collect the taxes of Bengal,
one of the richest provinces on earth.
A company now ruled millions of people, and its first priority was profit.
In 1770, a terrible famine struck Bengal. Some estimates say up to a third of the population
died. The company didn't cut its taxes. It raised them. In these same years, English
picked up a new word from India. Lute. From the Hindi, lute. Plunder. Not everyone gave
in. Tipu Sultan of Mysore fought the company with iron-cased rockets so good that the
copied them. In the Punjab, Ranjit Singh built a Sikh empire that kept the
company out for 40 years. He even got the Kohinoor. But after he died, the company
took the Punjab and the diamond went to Queen Victoria. Remember our question?
Every robber before had stayed and become part of India. This one kept its
headquarters in London. By the 1850s, the company controlled most of India and
soldiers it relied on most, the seapoys, were Indian. That was about to matter. A lot.
